title: The map of the piece
summary: Find the sections and where they repeat, draw the map, then play from memory using the map instead of the notes.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil
a ruler, for the science moment

figure.alt: Three boxes stacked, standing for the piece's three sections. The first and third are shaded the same, showing that section A repeats; the middle, unshaded, is section B. This is the map drawn before playing from memory.

steps.title: The map of the piece
steps.body:
A piece is not a long line of notes. It is a few sections, and most of them come back. Once you can see the map, the piece is shorter than it looks, and far easier to remember.

1. Play the piece and listen for where it repeats. Give each section a letter: A, B, then A again.
2. Draw the map on paper: the letters in order, with the bar number where each one starts.
3. Play the sections out of order: B, then A, then the ending. Start each one from your map, not from the top.
4. Close the page and play the piece from memory, using the map. When you get lost, look at the map, not the notes.

Memory works by structure. Nobody remembers two hundred notes; they remember three sections and how they join.

figure.alt: A keyboard spanning two octaves from C3 to B4. The lowest note, C3, on the left, and the highest note shown, B4, on the right, are highlighted, standing for the long, thick strings on the left and the short, thin strings on the right.

steps.title: Long strings, low notes
steps.body:
Look inside a piano if you can, or at a picture of one. The strings on the left, the low notes, are long and thick. The strings on the right, the high notes, are short and thin. That is not decoration. A longer or heavier string wiggles more slowly, and a slower wiggle is a lower note.

Predict first: hold a ruler flat on the table with most of it sticking out over the edge, and twang the end. Will a long overhang buzz lower or higher than a short one? Write your guess in the Practice log.

Measure: twang it with a long overhang, then slide it in so only a little sticks out, and twang again. Listen to the buzz.

Compare: was your guess right? A guitar player uses the same rule: pressing a string against the neck shortens the part that wiggles, and the note goes up. Teach it: explain to someone why the biggest instrument in an orchestra plays the lowest notes.

figure.alt: Three boxes stacked for the piece's sections, A, B and A again, the first and third shaded to show the repeat. Sections are played out of order, then the whole piece from memory using this map.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: find the sections, draw the map with letters and bar numbers
Sitting 2: play the sections out of order, starting each from the map
Sitting 3: page closed, play from memory with the map beside you
Sitting 4: page closed and map closed, the whole piece from memory, then once with the page
An old piece: draw its map from memory, then play it

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Say the name of the piece, then play it once through, hands in the frame. Slips stay in.
